opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the parts of the project I find most fascinating. Some quick context first: MrT5 is built on top of ByT5, which is a byte-level model. It doesn't use a tokenizer at all. It reads raw bytes. That's great for robustness and for handling any language, but byte sequences are long, so the model is slow and expensive. What MrT5 adds is a learned deletion mechanism. After a few early encoder layers, a gate decides which byte positions can be dropped. The remaining layers then run on a much shorter sequence.

What's interesting is that we never tell the model how to compress. We just give it a regularizer that encourages deletion, and it figures out on its own which bytes it can afford to throw away. Because those early layers have already done some contextual processing, information from the deleted bytes is merged into the ones that survive. So the model is really learning its own soft, contextual tokenization.

When we trained it multilingually, the deletion rates differed quite a bit across languages, and they tracked the structure of each writing system in sensible ways. For Latin-script languages like English or French, the model can delete a large fraction of bytes. It often keeps roughly one representative position per word or chunk and drops things like whitespace and predictable characters. For scripts where a single character spans multiple bytes in UTF-8, like Chinese, Japanese, or many Indic scripts, the pattern looks different. The model learns to collapse the redundant bytes within a character, and sometimes the effective rate ends up quite different from English. Nobody hand-designed any of that. It emerges from the training objective and the data.

To me, that's the exciting part. Subword tokenizers like BPE are fixed before training and are known to be unfair across languages. Lower-resource languages, or ones in non-Latin scripts, often get chopped into many more tokens, which makes them more expensive and sometimes worse in performance. With a learned, dynamic approach, the model can adapt its compression to the language and even to the specific context it's seeing. We're not all the way there yet, but it points toward a future where models decide for themselves how to segment input, instead of inheriting a static tokenizer's biases.

r001.rationale: The response says deletion rates differ across languages and that no language-specific compression instructions are given; the rates emerge from the training objective and data.

r002.rationale: It describes how Chinese script’s multibyte characters affect byte deletion, but does not say Chinese is compressed less than Latin-script languages because its script has greater information density.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the things that surprised us the most. So just to back up a little, the whole idea behind MrT5 is that byte-level models like ByT5 are great because they don't have a tokenizer, they just operate directly on UTF-8 bytes, but the problem is that your sequences get really, really long. And that's expensive. So we added this learned deletion mechanism, a gating layer, early in the encoder that decides which byte representations to drop, and then the rest of the encoder only processes the ones that survive. The model essentially learns its own form of tokenization, or compression, during training.

And what's interesting is that we don't tell it how much to delete per language. There's a regularizer that pushes toward a target deletion rate overall, but the model is free to allocate that however it wants across inputs. And what we saw is that it ends up compressing different languages by very different amounts, and that pattern tracks pretty closely with how efficiently UTF-8 encodes that script in the first place.

So English, or really any Latin-script language, is one byte per character, and the model learns to delete, I think somewhere around 50 percent or more of the bytes there. But then you look at something like Russian or Greek, where characters take two bytes, or Chinese or Japanese where it's three bytes per character, and the model deletes a much larger fraction. It's kind of recovering the redundancy that the encoding introduced. Those continuation bytes in a multi-byte character don't carry a lot of independent information once the earlier layers have already contextualized them, so the model learns it can get rid of them.

The thing I find really cool about that is it means the final sequence lengths across languages end up much more balanced than they were at the byte level. One of the long-standing complaints about subword tokenizers is this unfairness issue, where a sentence in English becomes thirty tokens and the same sentence in Burmese or Amharic becomes two hundred, so speakers of those languages are effectively paying more for the same content. MrT5 doesn't fully solve that, but it moves in the right direction, and it does it without anyone hand-designing the vocabulary. The model figured out where the redundancy was on its own.

The other piece I think is worth mentioning is that it's not purely a per-language thing either. Within a language, the deletion isn't uniform. It tends to keep bytes that are at the ends of words or at word boundaries and drop ones in the middle, which sort of looks like it's learning that the representation at the end of a span has already absorbed the earlier context. So it's doing something that resembles a tokenizer, but a contextual one, which is kind of the dream for this line of work.

r001.rationale: It says the model is not told how much to delete per language, yet learns different deletion amounts across languages.

r002.rationale: It says Chinese is compressed more than Latin-script text, attributing that to UTF-8’s multibyte encoding and redundant continuation bytes. It does not say Chinese is compressed less because its script is more information-dense.

astra-6.text:
What I find really interesting is that Mr. T5 can learn how much to compress depending on the language, rather than applying the same compression rate everywhere. It has this deletion mechanism that lets it shorten the sequence internally, and we can look at what it chooses to keep and what it chooses to delete.

That’s especially interesting across languages because the same amount of text—or the same number of bytes—doesn’t necessarily represent the same amount of information. Different writing systems and different morphological structures give you very different sequences. So the question is: can the model learn to account for those differences while preserving what it needs to perform the task?

And I’d be careful about interpreting deletion as saying that a character is unimportant. The model can move information into neighboring representations before deleting a position. It’s really learning where to concentrate information, which makes the compression behavior fascinating to study.

r001.rationale: The response says Mr. T5 learns how much to compress depending on the language, but does not state that this learning is implicit or that it receives no prior specifying different rates by language.

r002.rationale: It discusses differences in information density across writing systems generally, but does not say Mr. T5 compresses Chinese less than Latin-script languages or attribute that difference to Chinese script’s greater information density.

sol-6.1.text: What I find really interesting is that Mr. T5 can learn different compression patterns for different languages without us explicitly telling it which language it’s looking at. It learns to merge tokens based on what’s useful for the task. And because languages get split into tokens differently, the same amount of text can require very different sequence lengths. So the question is whether the model can learn to compensate for that—compressing more where the tokenization is more fragmented, while preserving the information it needs. That makes compression an interesting lens for studying what the model learns about linguistic structure.

r001.rationale: The response says Mr. T5 learns different compression patterns for different languages without being told which language it is seeing, communicating implicit language-specific compression rates without a prior specifying them.

r002.rationale: The response discusses tokenization and sequence lengths generally, but does not state that Chinese is compressed less than Latin-script languages because Chinese script is more information-dense.
